fields.meta_title: PT Intake Form Builder for Physical Therapists | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a PT intake form that asks where it hurts and how it started, then sends the therapist a summary before the first visit. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a PT Intake Form Therapists Read Before the Evaluation
fields.hero_description: Describe the questions your evaluations open with and the answers someone should see early. Emergent builds the PT intake form and the patient database behind it.
fields.features_heading: What a PT Intake Form Should Capture
fields.features_subheading: Each one answers a question the therapist would otherwise ask at the start of the evaluation.
fields.feature_1:
A body chart with a pain scale

Let patients tap where it hurts on a front and back body chart, then rate each spot from 0 to 10 at rest and with activity. The ratings print on the summary the therapist reads.
fields.feature_2:
Onset questions that branch

Ask when the problem started and what set it off. A fall opens questions about where and how it happened, and a sports injury asks about the sport and the position played.
fields.feature_3:
Goals in the patient's own words

Ask what the patient wants to do again, such as climb the stairs at home or lift a toddler. Each answer is saved word for word, ready for the therapist to set goals around it.
fields.feature_4:
Referral and protocol uploads

Collect the referring provider's name and a photo of the prescription, plus the surgeon's protocol after an operation. Every file is stored with that patient's intake record.
fields.feature_5:
Function questionnaires, totaled

Add a questionnaire your clinic already scores, such as the Lower Extremity Functional Scale. The form adds up all 20 items on submit and shows the total next to the pain ratings.
fields.feature_6:
Source code in your repository

Export the form and its patient database to your GitHub repository. Run it on your own servers, or have a developer connect it to the scheduling software your front desk uses.

fields.usecase_heading: PT Intake Forms by Clinic Type
fields.tab_content_1:
A one-page summary reaches the therapist the night before

Fairmount Physical Therapy sends the intake with each booking. Ana Ruiz marks her right shoulder on the body chart and rates it 6 out of 10 when reaching overhead. It started 3 weeks ago, after she painted a ceiling. Her therapist, Ben Cole, gets a one-page summary by email the evening before the visit.
fields.tab_content_2:
A parent's milestone ages, drawn on one timeline

Parents booking at Little Oak Pediatric Therapy enter the age in months when their child first sat, crawled and walked. They can attach a 30-second phone video of the child walking. Before the first session, Priya Shah sees those ages on one timeline beside the video and the parent's concern.
fields.tab_content_3:
Three weeks after ACL surgery, booked with the ACL lead

A soccer player opens the Summit Sports Rehab intake, enters the date of his ACL reconstruction and uploads the protocol his surgeon gave him. The form counts the weeks since the operation and books his evaluation with Marcus Lee, who carries the clinic's ACL caseload. The protocol is attached to the visit.
fields.tab_content_4:
Any patient with two falls gets the 60-minute slot

Harborview Physical Therapy gives a 60-minute balance evaluation to any new patient with two or more falls in the last 12 months. Everyone else keeps the standard 45-minute slot. The front desk sees the change on the schedule with the reason beside it, and the patient gets an updated confirmation.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a PT Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Work backward from the evaluation, then decide which answers should reach someone before the patient walks in.
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Mark answers that change a booking
fields.howto_step_1_des: Open a recent evaluation and list what the therapist asked before examining the patient. Each of those questions belongs on the form. A question nobody reads at the evaluation can come off, and a shorter form is easier to finish on a phone.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put onset near the top: the date, and what the patient was doing when the pain began. Follow-up questions branch from that answer. Pain ratings come next, at rest and during the activity that hurts most.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Pick the 0 to 10 scale and use it for every rating on the form. Mixing numbers with faces or words makes the ratings harder to compare when the therapist reassesses the patient later in the plan.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Name each answer that should change something before the visit, such as a recent operation or a history of falls. For each one, write down who hears about it and what moves on the schedule. Pick email or Slack for every alert.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your questions and those rules into the prompt in plain English. Emergent builds the form with a patient database behind it and sends the summary emails. When a rule changes later, prompt again and the live form updates to match.
fields.howto_step_6_des: End with your cancellation policy and consent to evaluation and treatment, then a signature field. Keep each policy to a sentence or two. Ask whoever handles compliance at your clinic to read the wording before the form goes out to patients.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Fill it once as a test patient
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before sending the link, fill the form yourself as a post-op patient who reports two falls. Check that the summary email arrives and the booking moves to the longer slot. Then send the link with every booking confirmation.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is clinic PDFs (a hospital outpatient packet, a pediatric center, two private practices), a sports clinic's forms page, Jotform's template, a generic patient template and one PT forms vendor. All of them print the same history questions and stop. This page treats the PT intake as the subjective half of the evaluation: where it hurts, how it started, what makes it worse and what the patient wants back. It then shows four physical therapy settings whose online form turns those answers into something a therapist or front desk acts on before the first visit: an orthopedic summary read the night before, a pediatric milestone timeline, a post-op athlete matched to the ACL lead, and a falls answer that books a longer balance evaluation.
